message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a C++ library black-box. The compiled binary is /workspace/dataset/test13_executable.
It takes ONE command-line argument (call it W) and, only when argc > 1, prints exactly 13 lines:
  line 1  = Inflector::pluralize(W)
  line 2  = Inflector::singularize(W + "s")
  line 3  = Inflector::camelize("test_" + W)
  line 4  = Inflector::underscore("Test" + W)
  line 5  = Inflector::classify(W + "_table")
  line 6  = Inflector::tableize(W + "Class")
  line 7  = Inflector::humanize(W + "_id")
  line 8  = Inflector::titleize(W)
  line 9  = Inflector::dasherize(W)
  line 10 = Inflector::parameterize("The " + W + " Test")
  line 11 = Inflector::upcase(W)
  line 12 = Inflector::downcase(W)
  line 13 = Inflector::capitalize(W)
Each line is followed by "\n" (std::endl).

Probe by running the binary and reading the relevant line, e.g.:
  /workspace/dataset/test13_executable 'someword' | sed -n 2p
Use printf/quoting carefully so W is passed verbatim (including empty string, spaces, punctuation, UTF-8, backslashes).
Note you can only observe a function through its fixed input template, so choose W to synthesize the inputs you need
(e.g. to test singularize on "cities", pass W='citie'; to test underscore on "TestFooBar", pass W='FooBar').

DO NOT read any C++ source (none is present anyway) and do not disassemble. Infer purely from input/output behavior.
Run MANY probes - dozens to hundreds. Be systematic and exhaustive; brute-force over suffixes/character classes.
Report byte-exact observations. Where you cannot observe a behavior through the template, say so explicitly
and mark it UNOBSERVABLE rather than guessing silently.

YOUR AREA: upcase (line 11), downcase (line 12), capitalize (line 13).
Reconnaissance: upcase("café")="CAFé" (the two UTF-8 bytes of é unchanged), upcase("ÄÖÜ")="ÄÖÜ",
downcase("ÄÖÜ")="ÄÖÜ", capitalize("cAT")="Cat", capitalize("ABC")="Abc", capitalize("FooBar")="Foobar",
capitalize("foo_bar")="Foo_bar", capitalize("A B")="A b", capitalize("  lead")="  lead",
capitalize("trail  ")="Trail  ", capitalize("  ")="  ", capitalize("")="" .
Hypothesis: all three are pure per-BYTE ASCII-only case mapping (bytes 0x80-0xFF untouched, i.e. the C locale),
capitalize = uppercase first byte + lowercase all remaining bytes.
Your job: verify EXHAUSTIVELY over the byte space. Write a loop that, for every byte value from 0x01 to 0xFF
(skip 0x00 since it cannot be passed in argv, and handle 0x0A newline specially because it shifts line numbering),
passes a W containing that byte in a safe context (e.g. W = 'a' + byte + 'z', built with printf) and compares
lines 11/12/13 against the pure-ASCII-mapping prediction. Use od -An -tx1 to compare byte-exactly.
Report any byte where the binary deviates from pure ASCII-only mapping.
Also confirm capitalize's behavior when the first byte is not a letter, and on 1-byte and empty inputs.
Be careful with shell quoting; prefer building args via printf and passing with "$(printf ...)" or use a small
helper script. Note that a raw newline byte inside W makes the physical line count exceed 13 - handle it by
reasoning about the full output rather than sed line numbers.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.area: Inflector::upcase (line 11), Inflector::downcase (line 12), Inflector::capitalize (line 13) — verified against /workspace/dataset/test13_executable via ~86,000 binary invocations / ~259,000 byte-exact line comparisons, with ZERO deviations from the pure per-byte ASCII-only model. Coverage: (a) all 255 passable byte values 0x01-0xFF placed in first, middle, last, and sole position (1020 inputs); (b) the COMPLETE exhaustive 2-byte input space, all 255x255 = 65025 inputs; (c) 3-byte exhaustive over a 25-byte "interesting" alphabet (15625 inputs, incl. 0x09/0x0A/0x0D/0x20/0x40/0x41/0x5A/0x5B/0x5F/0x60/0x61/0x7A/0x7B/0x7F/0x80/0xA9/0xC3/0xDF/0xFF); (d) 2500 random strings of length 0-64 over bytes 0x01-0xFF; (e) long strings up to 4000 bytes; (f) newline-containing inputs (handled by counting physical lines from the END of the output, not sed line numbers); (g) empty string; (h) 25 hand-picked UTF-8 / Latin-1 / locale-trap sequences; (i) idempotence over 300 random 8-byte strings for all three functions; (j) locale invariance under LC_ALL/LANG/LC_CTYPE = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8. The reconnaissance hypothesis is CONFIRMED exactly as stated.

rules.pattern: upcase: input byte b with 0x61 <= b <= 0x7A ('a'..'z')
rules.note: The ONLY transformation upcase ever performs. Applied independently to every byte position (first, middle, last, sole). Empirically derived table has exactly these 26 entries: 61->41 62->42 63->43 64->44 65->45 66->46 67->47 68->48 69->49 6a->4a 6b->4b 6c->4c 6d->4d 6e->4e 6f->4f 70->50 71->51 72->52 73->53 74->54 75->55 76->56 77->57 78->58 79->59 7a->5a.

rules.pattern: downcase: input byte b with 0x41 <= b <= 0x5A ('A'..'Z')
rules.note: The ONLY transformation downcase ever performs. Applied independently to every byte position. Empirically derived table has exactly these 26 entries: 41->61 42->62 43->63 44->64 45->65 46->66 47->67 48->68 49->69 4a->6a 4b->6b 4c->6c 4d->6d 4e->6e 4f->6f 50->70 51->71 52->72 53->73 54->74 55->75 56->76 57->77 58->78 59->79 5a->7a.

rules.pattern: any byte b in 0x01..0x40, 0x5B..0x60, or 0x7B..0xFF (all 203 non-ASCII-letter passable bytes)
rules.note: Verified for ALL 255 passable byte values in first, middle, last and sole position, and across the complete 255x255 two-byte input space. Includes every high byte 0x80-0xFF, so UTF-8 lead and continuation bytes, raw Latin-1 bytes, controls (0x01-0x1F incl. 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0D CR), space 0x20, all punctuation, digits 0x30-0x39, and the four near-miss boundary bytes 0x40 '@', 0x5B '[', 0x60 '`', 0x7B '{' are all untouched.

rules.pattern: capitalize: byte at index 0 of a non-empty input
rules.replacement: ascii_upper_byte(byte)  i.e. a-z -> A-Z, everything else identity
rules.note: Strictly index 0 of the BYTE string. Observable that it really is uppercased (not merely left alone): capitalize('z') = 'Z', capitalize('a'+0x61) = 'Aa'. When index 0 is not a lowercase ASCII letter it passes through: '1abc'->'1abc', '_ABC'->'_abc', '@ABC'->'@abc', '[ABC'->'[abc', '`ABC'->'`abc', '{ABC'->'{abc', 0x7F+'ABC'->0x7F+'abc', 0xFF+'ABC'->0xFF+'abc', 0x09+'TAB'+0x09 -> 0x09+'tab'+0x09.

rules.replacement: ascii_lower_byte(byte)  i.e. A-Z -> a-z, everything else identity
rules.note: Unconditionally lowercased regardless of what precedes it. Kills any word-boundary theory: 'A B' -> 'A b', 'FooBar' -> 'Foobar', 'MiXeD_CaSe-99' -> 'Mixed_case-99', 'abc123!@#XYZ' -> 'Abc123!@#xyz'. Also lowercases across an embedded newline: $'a\x0AZ' -> $'A\x0Az'.

Confirmed: with W='' lines 11, 12 and 13 are all zero-length (each still terminated by the endl '\n'). Whether this is an explicit empty() guard or a natural consequence of the loop bounds is UNOBSERVABLE.

rules.pattern: capitalize: leading whitespace is NOT skipped
rules.replacement: index 0 is the space itself; no letter gets promoted
rules.note: capitalize('  lead') = '  lead' (byte 0 is 0x20, ascii_upper_byte(0x20)=0x20; 'l' at index 2 is merely lowercased, i.e. unchanged). Contrast capitalize('trail  ') = 'Trail  ' where trailing spaces are preserved verbatim. capitalize('  ') = '  '.

rules.pattern: multibyte UTF-8 sequences (any length: 2, 3 or 4 bytes)
rules.replacement: passed through byte-for-byte, never case-mapped, never re-encoded, never expanded
rules.note: 'caf'+0xC3 0xA9 -> upcase 'CAF'+0xC3 0xA9 (e-acute survives), 'CAF'+0xC3 0x89 -> downcase 'caf'+0xC3 0x89 (E-acute survives), 0xC3 0x84 0xC3 0x96 0xC3 0x9C ('AOU'-umlaut) identical under all three, 0xCE 0xB1 0xCE 0xB2 0xCE 0xB3 (Greek abg) identical, 0xC4 0xB0 (Turkish dotted I) identical, 0xC7 0x85 (Dz titlecase) identical, 0xC3 0x9F (sharp s) identical (no ->SS expansion), plus tested: micro sign, capital sharp s, long s, IJ ligature, fi ligature, Cyrillic, CJK, fullwidth, 4-byte emoji, 4-byte Deseret -- all byte-identical.

Byte-identical output under C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8 for W = $'i\xC3\xA9I\xC3\x89\xC3\x9F'. Notably tr_TR.UTF-8 still gives 0x69 -> 0x49 ('i'->'I'), never 'İ'. Consistent with the program never calling setlocale, so the C locale is in force permanently.

evidence.arg: $'a\x0AZ'  (embedded newline; lines located by counting from END of output, 2 physical lines per logical line)
z  -- proves capitalize really DOES uppercase index 0
$'i\xC3\xA9I\xC3\x89\xC3\x9F' run with LC_ALL=LANG=LC_CTYPE=tr_TR.UTF-8 -- 'i' still maps to 'I' (0x69->0x49), never 'İ' (0xC4 0xB0)
$'i\xC3\xA9I\xC3\x89\xC3\x9F' with LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 -- 'I' still maps to 'i' (0x49->0x69), never dotless 0xC4 0xB1
$'i\xC3\xA9I\xC3\x89\xC3\x9F' with LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 (byte-identical under C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8 too)

unobservable: EMBEDDED NUL BYTE (0x00): cannot be passed inside argv (execve terminates each argument at the first NUL), so the behavior of upcase/downcase/capitalize on a string containing 0x00 is UNOBSERVABLE through this template. In particular it is UNOBSERVABLE whether the functions iterate over std::string::size() bytes (and would therefore case-map past an interior NUL) or stop at a NUL terminator. Confirmed 0x00 is unreachable: only 0x01..0xFF were testable.

IMPLEMENTATION MECHANISM of the byte mapping: whether the binary uses hardcoded range arithmetic (b >= 'a' && b <= 'z' ? b - 32 : b), a 256-entry lookup table, ::toupper/::tolower from <cctype> under the never-changed "C" locale, or std::toupper(c, std::locale::classic()) is UNOBSERVABLE -- all four are byte-for-byte identical on every reachable input. I tried to break the tie by forcing LC_ALL/LANG/LC_CTYPE to tr_TR.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, C.UTF-8 and C; output was byte-identical in all five, which is consistent with the program never calling setlocale (so a <cctype> implementation can never be induced to behave non-ASCII).

SIGNEDNESS of the internal char type for bytes >= 0x80: whether the implementation passes a signed char (negative value, technically UB for ::toupper) or promotes to unsigned char is UNOBSERVABLE, because all 128 bytes 0x80-0xFF are identity-mapped under either interpretation in the C locale, and I confirmed all 128 are identity-mapped.

WHETHER capitalize INTERNALLY CALLS upcase/downcase: capitalize(s) == upcase(s[0:1]) + downcase(s[1:]) holds for every input tested, but whether the binary literally composes the two public functions, calls a shared per-byte helper, or has a fused inline loop is UNOBSERVABLE.

WHETHER capitalize HAS AN EXPLICIT EMPTY GUARD: capitalize("") == "" is observed, but whether that comes from an `if (s.empty()) return s;` early-out or simply from the loop body never executing is UNOBSERVABLE.

IN-PLACE vs COPY SEMANTICS, and the C++ signatures: whether these take/return std::string by value, const-reference, or char*, whether they mutate the argument in place, and whether they are static members or free functions in a namespace, are all UNOBSERVABLE from stdout bytes alone (and I was instructed not to read source or disassemble).
WHETHER upcase/downcase/capitalize ARE THEMSELVES USED BY THE OTHER TEN INFLECTOR FUNCTIONS: outside my assigned area and not determinable from lines 11-13.

BEHAVIOR AT EXTREME LENGTHS: I verified up to 4000 bytes. Lengths beyond the kernel's per-argument limit (MAX_ARG_STRLEN, typically 131072 bytes) cannot be passed at all, so any allocation-failure / length-overflow behavior is UNOBSERVABLE.

LOCALE-DEPENDENT BEHAVIOR IF setlocale WERE CALLED: since the program appears never to call setlocale, I cannot observe what the case mapping would do under a non-C LC_CTYPE. If the implementation is <cctype>-based, such behavior exists in principle but is unreachable through this binary. Marked UNOBSERVABLE rather than asserting the mapping is hardcoded.
EXCEPTION / ERROR PATHS: no input among ~86,000 probes produced a crash, non-zero exit, stderr output, or a line count other than 13 logical lines, so no error path is observable.

TITLECASE/UNICODE-EXPANSION PATHS: because no input ever changed length, I can only state that expansion never happens for any reachable input; whether the code contains dormant multi-byte logic is UNOBSERVABLE.
